subject: English
topic: Who vs Whom: subject vs object case
prompt: Fill in: The teacher to ___ I spoke was very kind.
explain: A preposition is followed by the object form 'whom'. 'That' cannot follow a preposition.

subject: English
topic: Who vs Whom: subject vs object case
prompt: Fill in: ___ do you think won the quiz?
explain: 'Do you think' is parenthetical. 'Who' is the subject of 'won'.

subject: English
topic: Who vs Whom: subject vs object case
prompt: Fill in: The man ___ I thought was a thief turned out to be a guard.
explain: 'I thought' is parenthetical; 'who' is the subject of 'was'.

subject: English
topic: Who vs Whom: subject vs object case
prompt: Fill in: Give the prize to ___ deserves it most.
explain: 'Whoever' is the subject of 'deserves'. The preposition 'to' governs the whole clause, not the pronoun.

subject: English
prompt: Fill in: The poet ___ poems we studied last year has passed away.
explain: Possession by a person needs 'whose' + noun (whose poems).

subject: English
prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a relative pronoun for a non-living thing?
options: The table whose legs are broken is old.
The table which legs are broken is old.
The table that legs are broken is old.
The table who legs are broken is old.
explain: 'Whose' can show possession for things; 'that' and 'which' have no possessive form.

subject: English
prompt: In 'The girl who's singing is my cousin', 'who's' stands for:
explain: 'Who's' is a contraction of 'who is' or 'who has', never possessive.

subject: English
prompt: He failed the test, ___ surprised everyone.
explain: Only 'which' (after a comma) can refer to a whole preceding clause; 'that' and 'what' cannot.

subject: English
prompt: The room in ___ we met was very small.
explain: A preposition placed before the relative pronoun takes 'which' for things; 'that' cannot follow it.

subject: English
prompt: The table, the legs ___ are broken, was sold cheaply.
explain: For a possessive relation with things, 'of which' is used (or 'whose'); 'of whom' is for people.

subject: English
prompt: 'Which' can be omitted only when it is the ___ of a defining clause.
explain: Object 'which' may be dropped: 'The book I bought'. Subject 'which' must stay.

subject: English
topic: That: usage and where it is mandatory
prompt: Fill in: 'This is the best film ___ I have ever seen.' Which relative pronoun is preferred after a superlative?
explain: After a superlative, 'that' is the preferred relative pronoun.

subject: English
topic: That: usage and where it is mandatory
prompt: Fill in: 'All ___ glitters is not gold.'
explain: After 'all', 'that' is used; 'what' already includes an antecedent.

subject: English
topic: That: usage and where it is mandatory
prompt: Fill in: 'The boy and his dog ___ were rescued are safe.'
explain: With an antecedent that is both a person and an animal, 'that' is used.

subject: English
topic: That: usage and where it is mandatory
prompt: 'That' cannot be used as a relative pronoun in which type of clause?
explain: Non-defining (comma-marked) clauses take who/which, never 'that'.

subject: English
topic: That: usage and where it is mandatory
prompt: Fill in: 'He is the only person ___ can solve this problem.'
explain: After 'the only', 'the same', 'the very', 'that' is preferred.

subject: English
topic: That: usage and where it is mandatory
prompt: Fill in: 'He was the first man ___ reached the summit.'
explain: 'That' is preferred after ordinals like first and last.

subject: English
topic: That not after comma or preposition
prompt: The Taj Mahal, ___ was built by Shah Jahan, is in Agra.
explain: A comma-set (non-defining) clause cannot use 'that'; it takes 'which'.

subject: English
topic: That not after comma or preposition
prompt: My sister, ___ lives in Pune, is a doctor.
explain: A comma-set clause about a person (subject) takes 'who', not 'that'.

subject: English
prompt: In a non-defining clause, the relative pronoun, even as an object, ___.
explain: Omission of the relative pronoun is possible only in defining clauses, not in non-defining ones.

subject: English
prompt: If a non-defining clause is removed from a sentence, the remaining sentence ___.
explain: A non-defining clause only adds extra information; the main clause stands on its own.

subject: English
prompt: Which sentence has a defining clause, so it needs NO commas?
options: The boy who won the prize is my cousin.
My mother, who is a teacher, is kind.
Mr. Rao, who won the prize, is my cousin.
Mumbai, which is a port, is busy.
explain: 'The boy who won' identifies which boy, so it is defining and takes no commas.

subject: English
prompt: He is one of those students who ___ always punctual.
formula: one of those + plural noun + who + plural verb
explain: 'Who' refers to plural 'students' (not 'one'), so the verb is plural: are.

subject: English
prompt: She is the only one of the girls who ___ passed the test.
formula: the only one of + plural + who + singular verb
explain: With 'the only one', 'who' refers to 'one', so the verb is singular: has.

subject: English
prompt: It is I who ___ responsible for this mistake.
explain: The relative verb agrees with the antecedent 'I' (first person): am.

subject: English
prompt: It is you who ___ to blame for the delay.
explain: Antecedent 'you' takes 'are' in the relative clause.

subject: English
prompt: In a relative clause, the verb agrees in number and person with the ___.
explain: A relative pronoun takes the number and person of its antecedent.

subject: English
prompt: Everyone who ___ invited to the party came on time.
explain: 'Everyone' is singular, so the relative clause takes a singular verb: was.

subject: English
topic: One of those who + plural verb
prompt: Fill in: He is one of those leaders who keep ___ promises.
explain: 'Who' has a plural antecedent, so the pronoun must be plural: their.

subject: English
prompt: Which sentence is grammatically incorrect?
options: The town that he lives in is small.
The town in which he lives is small.
The town which he lives in is small.
The town in that he lives is small.
explain: 'That' cannot directly follow a preposition; use 'which' or 'whom'.

subject: English
prompt: Fill in the blank: She has two sons, both of ___ are engineers.
explain: 'Of' is a preposition, so the personal pronoun after it is 'whom'.

subject: English
prompt: Fill in the blank: He bought several books, none of ___ were useful.
explain: For things, 'which' follows the preposition: 'none of which'.

subject: English
prompt: Spot the error: "The street where he lives in is very quiet."
explain: 'Where' already means 'in which', so the extra 'in' is redundant.

subject: English
prompt: In which sentence is 'what' a relative pronoun meaning 'that which'?
options: What a lovely day it is!
What time does the train leave?
explain: 'He bought what he needed' = 'that which he needed'; others are exclamatory or interrogative uses.

subject: English
prompt: "She eats whatever is served." Here 'whatever' is closest in meaning to:
explain: Whatever acts as a compound relative: 'anything that', and it starts a noun clause.

subject: English
prompt: Choose the correct form: "Invite ___ you like to the party."
explain: Inside its clause, 'whomever' is the object of 'like' (you like whomever), so the objective form is used.

subject: English
prompt: Spot the error: "The watch that I bought it yesterday is costly."
options: 'it' is redundant; 'that' already is the object
explain: The relative pronoun already stands for the object, so repeating 'it' is redundant.

subject: English
prompt: Spot the error: "She gave a book to the girl which was torn."
explain: A relative clause must stay next to its antecedent; 'which was torn' refers to 'book'.

subject: English
prompt: Spot the error: "My friend, who he lives in Delhi, called me."
explain: 'Who' is already the subject of 'lives'; adding 'he' duplicates the subject.

subject: English
prompt: He may arrive late, ___ case we shall begin without him.
explain: 'In which case' is a fixed phrase: preposition + which + noun, as a connective relative.

subject: English
prompt: Spot the error: "I still remember the time where we first met."
explain: The antecedent 'time' denotes a time, so the relative adverb must be 'when', not 'where'.

subject: English
prompt: Spot the error: "That is the reason because he left early."
explain: After the noun 'reason', the relative adverb 'why' (or 'that') is used, not 'because'.

subject: English
prompt: In "This is the reason why she resigned", the word 'why' can be:
explain: In defining clauses, 'why' after 'reason' may be omitted or replaced by 'that'.

subject: English
prompt: Fill in: "She moved to Pune, ___ her sister lives."
explain: Non-defining clause after a place name takes 'where'; 'which' would need a preposition.

subject: English
prompt: Fill in: "There are times ___ silence is the best reply."
explain: 'Times' is a time noun, so the relative adverb 'when' is used.

subject: English
prompt: Which relative pronoun can NEVER be omitted, even in a defining clause?
explain: Whose, being a possessive determiner, cannot be dropped, unlike an object who, whom, which or that.

subject: English
prompt: 'The students, who were late, were punished' implies that ___ .
explain: Commas make the clause non-defining: it adds information about all the students, not a subset.

subject: English
prompt: Spot the error: 'Rahul, who is my cousin lives in Pune.'
explain: A mid-sentence non-defining clause needs a pair of commas, one before and one after.

subject: English
prompt: Removing a defining relative clause from a sentence usually ___ .
explain: A defining clause identifies which person or thing is meant; without it the noun is vague.

subject: English
prompt: In 'The boy who won the race is my cousin', 'who' can be replaced by ___ .
explain: In a defining clause, 'that' can replace 'who' or 'which'.

subject: English
prompt: In speech, a non-defining clause is usually marked by ___ .
explain: Commas in writing correspond to pauses in speech; a defining clause is spoken without a break.

subject: English
prompt: A non-defining clause can often be paraphrased by joining the sentences with ___ .
explain: 'Ravi, who is tall, plays well' ≈ 'Ravi is tall and plays well': it just adds extra information.

subject: English
prompt: 'The boy who is sitting there is my cousin' can be shortened to ___ .
options: The boy sat there is my cousin.
The boy to sit there is my cousin.
The boy who sitting there is my cousin.
The boy sitting there is my cousin.
explain: 'who is' + present participle can be reduced to the participle alone.

subject: English
prompt: Which sentence is INCORRECT because of a wrongly omitted relative pronoun?
options: The house he lives in is old.
The house in which he lives is old.
The house in he lives is old.
The house that he lives in is old.
explain: When the preposition comes before the pronoun, the pronoun cannot be omitted: 'in which'.

subject: English
prompt: Best correction of: "A man was arrested who had stolen my car."
options: A man was arrested who he had stolen my car.
A man was arrested which had stolen my car.
A man who had stolen my car was arrested.
A man was arrested, whom had stolen my car.
explain: The relative clause must stand next to its antecedent 'man'.
